name: 陳柔妃
objective:
This course is designed to help graduate students master advanced techniques in geological field observation, data collection, and synthesis. Unlike introductory field courses, this curriculum focuses on integrating multidisciplinary data—including structural geology, stratigraphy, geomorphology, and remote sensing—to solve complex geological problems. Students will move beyond simple identification to perform kinematic analysis, stratigraphic correlation in tectonically active settings, and geological hazard assessments. The course emphasizes professional-grade mapping, the use of digital field tools, and the production of high-quality scientific reports suitable for professional or academic publication.

Learning Objectives
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
Execute high-resolution structural and lithological mapping in complex terrains.
Construct detailed stratigraphic logs and interpret depositional environments.
Utilize advanced GPS, GIS, and remote sensing tools for real-time digital mapping.
Conduct systematic geological hazard assessments, including landslide and seismic risk evaluations.
Synthesize field data into comprehensive geological maps and cross-sections.
Demonstrate professional standards in field safety, ethics, and scientific communication.
課程進度(1-16週):
Week 1: Introduction, Ethics, and Field Safety
Overview of graduate-level field expectations. Discussion on field ethics, land access, and environmental preservation. Comprehensive safety training, including wilderness first aid basics and emergency communication protocols.
Week 2: Advanced Lithology and Mineral Identification
Field identification of rock-forming minerals and textures in igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks. Focus on identifying diagnostic features under varying weathering conditions and light.
Week 3: Stratigraphic Principles and High-Resolution Logging
Techniques for measuring stratigraphic sections. Recording sedimentological structures, grain size variations, and fossil content. Introduction to sequence stratigraphy in a field context.
Week 4: Structural Geology I: Brittle Deformation
Field observation of faults, joints, and shear zones. Measuring orientation data (strike/dip, trend/plunge) and performing kinematic analysis using slickenlines and offset markers.
Week 5: Structural Geology II: Ductile Deformation and Folding
Mapping folded terrains. Identifying axial plane foliations, lineations, and parasitic folds. Constructing stereonets in the field to predict large-scale structures.
Week 6: Geomorphological Observation and Quaternary Mapping
Identifying landforms and surface processes. Mapping alluvial fans, river terraces, and glacial features. Understanding the relationship between tectonics and landscape evolution.
Week 7: Remote Sensing and GIS Integration
Pre-field analysis using satellite imagery, LiDAR, and Digital Elevation Models (DEM). Learning to overlay geological data on digital platforms to identify large-scale lineaments.
Week 8: Digital Mapping Tools and GPS Navigation
Hands-on training with digital mapping software. Integrating real-time GPS data with geological layers. Managing digital databases and ensuring data redundancy in the field.
Week 9: Mid-term Field Assessment
A full-day independent mapping exercise at a local site. Students must produce a preliminary map and a brief structural interpretation within a set timeframe.
Week 10: Geological Hazard Assessment: Landslides
Field identification of unstable slopes. Mapping tension cracks, hummocky topography, and drainage patterns. Introduction to rock mass rating (RMR) and slope stability evaluation.
Week 11: Geological Hazard Assessment: Seismic and Volcanic
Identifying active fault traces and paleoseismic evidence. Field recognition of volcanic hazards, including pyroclastic flow deposits and lahar paths.
Week 12: Igneous and Metamorphic Complex Mapping
Specialized techniques for mapping non-stratiform bodies. Identifying plutonic boundaries, metamorphic zones, and migmatitic structures.
Week 13: Hydrogeological Field Observations
Identifying aquifers and aquitards in the field. Mapping springs, seepages, and karst features. Understanding the influence of geological structures on groundwater flow.
Week 14: Data Synthesis and Cross-section Construction
Workshop on integrating disparate field data. Learning the techniques of balanced cross-section construction and 3D geological modeling based on surface observations.
Week 15: Scientific Report Writing and Professional Standards
Guidelines for drafting professional geological reports. Emphasis on clear descriptions, logical interpretations, and the proper use of citations and appendices.
Week 16: Pre-Camp Logistics and Project Planning
Final preparations for the overnight field camp. Distribution of regional data, team assignments, and development of a specific mapping strategy for the target area.
Week 17: Flexible Week I – Overnight Field Camp
Execution of the 3-day, 2-night intensive field mapping project. This week is dedicated to immersive field data collection and evening synthesis sessions. (See Itinerary below).
Week 18: Flexible Week II – Final Data Processing and Presentation
Post-camp laboratory work. Finalizing digital maps, refining cross-sect

materials:
Recommended Textbooks for Advanced Field Geology
The following list of recommended textbooks and academic resources has been curated to support graduate students in mastering the multi-disciplinary techniques required for advanced geological field observation, structural analysis, and hazard assessment.
Field Geology & Mapping
Coe, A. L. (Ed.). (2010). Geological field techniques. Wiley-Blackwell.
Jerram, D., & Petford, N. (2011). The field description of igneous rocks (2nd ed.). Wiley-Blackwell.
Structural Geology
Davis, G. H., Reynolds, S. J., & Kluth, C. (2012). Structural geology of rocks and regions (3rd ed.). Wiley.
Fossen, H. (2016). Structural geology (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press.
Stratigraphy
Catuneanu, O., Abreu, V., Bhattacharya, J. P., Blum, M. D., Dalrymple, R. W., Eriksson, P. G., Fielding, C. R., Fisher, W. L., Galloway, W. E., Gibling, M. R., Giles, K. A., Holbrook, J. M., Jordan, R., Kendall, C. G. S. C., Macurda, B., Martinsen, O. J., Miall, A. D., Neal, J. E., Nummedal, D., ... Winker, C. D. (2009). Towards the standardization of sequence stratigraphy. Earth-Science Reviews, 92(1–2), 1–33. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.earscirev.2008.10.003
Miall, A. D. (2000). Principles of sedimentary basin analysis (3rd ed.). Springer.
Geomorphology
Anderson, R. S., & Anderson, S. P. (2010). Geomorphology: The mechanics and chemistry of landscapes. Cambridge University Press.
Burbank, D. W., & Anderson, R. S. (2011). Tectonic geomorphology (2nd ed.). Wiley-Blackwell.
Remote Sensing & GIS
Kennedy, M. D. (2013). Introducing geographic information systems with ArcGIS (3rd ed.). Wiley.
Lillesand, T., Kiefer, R. W., & Chipman, J. (2015). Remote sensing and image interpretation (7th ed.). Wiley.
Geological Hazards
Keller, E. A., & Pinter, N. (2002). Active tectonics: Earthquakes, uplift, and landscape (2nd ed.). Prentice Hall.
Turner, A. K., & Schuster, R. L. (Eds.). (1996). Landslides: Investigation and mitigation (Special Report 247). Transportation Research Board, National Academy Press.
